question: What is CSRF and how does it work?
title: CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: **Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)** is an attack that tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an **unwanted state-changing request** to a site where they're already authenticated. Because browsers **automatically attach cookies** to requests, a malicious page can submit a form or fire a request to your bank/app and it rides on the victim's session. CSRF exploits **ambient authority** (cookies), so it only affects **cookie/session-based** apps — and the fix is an **anti-CSRF token** the attacker can't know, plus `SameSite` cookies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand CSRF abuses automatic cookie sending to forge authenticated requests, and that it targets state-changing actions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing CSRF with XSS; thinking it steals data (it forges actions); not knowing it only applies when auth rides on cookies
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain 'ambient authority' — the browser sends the cookie regardless of who initiated the request — and that this is why token-based APIs are largely immune

sections.title: What CSRF Is and Why It Works
sections.content:
**Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)** tricks a victim's browser into making a **state-changing request** to a site where the victim is already logged in. The attacker doesn't steal credentials — they **abuse the session that already exists**.

The mechanism is **ambient authority**: browsers **automatically attach the session cookie** to any request to a domain, regardless of which page initiated it. So if you're logged into your bank in one tab and visit a malicious page in another, that page can submit a hidden form to `bank.com/transfer` and your browser **dutifully attaches your bank cookie** — the bank sees a valid, authenticated request.

The critical insight: CSRF targets **actions, not data** (it forges a transfer, a password change, a delete), and it only works when authentication **rides on cookies** automatically. That's why it's distinct from XSS, and why **token-based APIs using the `Authorization` header are largely immune**. The standard defense is an **anti-CSRF token** the attacker's page can't read, reinforced by **`SameSite` cookies**.

sections.title: How a CSRF Attack Unfolds
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[Victim logs into bank.com
session cookie set] --> B[Victim visits
malicious site in another tab] B --> C[Malicious page auto-submits
hidden form to bank.com/transfer] C --> D[Browser attaches bank.com
cookie automatically] D --> E{Server checks
anti-CSRF token?} E -->|No token / not validated| F[Transfer executes
as the victim] E -->|Token required + valid| G[Request rejected 403
attacker can't supply token] ```

sections.title: Vulnerable: state-changing GET / no CSRF token
Safe: POST + CSRF token (Spring Security default)
Common Mistakes
sections.content: - **Confusing CSRF with XSS**: XSS runs script in the browser; CSRF forges a request using an existing session. Different attacks. - **Thinking CSRF steals data**: it forges **state-changing actions** (transfer, delete, change email) — the response usually isn't even read. - **Using GET for state changes**: any ``/link can trigger it. Mutations must be POST/PUT/DELETE. - **Disabling CSRF on a cookie-based app**: removes the protection. Only disable for stateless token APIs. - **Believing HTTPS stops CSRF**: encryption doesn't matter — the request is still validly authenticated.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **CSRF forces a logged-in user's browser to send an unwanted state-changing request.**
- It works via **ambient authority** — browsers auto-attach session cookies to every request.
- It targets **actions, not data**, and only affects **cookie/session-based** authentication.
- The fix is an **anti-CSRF token** the attacker can't read, plus **`SameSite` cookies**.
- **Token-based (JWT in `Authorization` header) APIs are largely immune** because nothing is auto-attached.
- Never expose **state changes over GET**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Cross-Site Request Forgery, or CSRF, is an attack that tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending a state-changing request to a site where they're already authenticated. The key thing is that the attacker isn't stealing the user's password or session — they're abusing a session that already exists. So it's about forging an action, not stealing data.

The reason it works comes down to how browsers handle cookies, which is sometimes called ambient authority. A browser automatically attaches the session cookie to any request going to a domain, no matter which page started that request. So imagine you're logged into your bank in one tab, and then you visit a malicious page in another tab. That page can quietly submit a hidden form, or even just load an image, that points at your bank's transfer endpoint. Your browser sees a request to the bank and helpfully attaches your bank cookie, so the server sees a perfectly valid, authenticated request and executes the transfer as you.

The important distinctions for an interview are: CSRF targets actions like transfers, deletes, or changing your email — not reading data — and it only works when authentication rides on cookies that the browser sends automatically. That's why it's different from XSS, and it's also why stateless APIs that send a JWT in the Authorization header are largely immune: that header isn't attached automatically, so a malicious page can't forge it. The standard defense for cookie-based apps is an anti-CSRF token — a secret value embedded in the form that the attacker's page can't read because of the same-origin policy — and Spring Security turns this on by default. I'd also use SameSite cookies and never expose a state change over a GET request.

beats.label: the exploit
beats.content: Imagine you're logged into bank.com. Your browser holds a session cookie. Now you open evil.com in another tab. That page has a hidden form that POSTs to bank.com/transfer. When the page loads, the form auto-submits. Your browser obediently attaches the bank.com session cookie to that cross-origin request. Bank.com sees a valid authenticated request and processes the transfer.

beats.label: two defenses
beats.content: CSRF tokens stop this by embedding a random secret value in every form. Attacker on evil.com can't read that value thanks to Same Origin Policy, so their forged form is missing the token and the server rejects it. The SameSite cookie attribute is a browser-level defense: SameSite=Strict means the cookie is never sent on cross-site requests at all.

beats.label: sharp edge
beats.content: sharp edge: CSRF doesn't require JavaScript. A plain HTML image tag like img src pointing at a state-changing GET endpoint is enough. That's why GET requests should never cause side effects.

question: How does a CSRF token work?
title: CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: An **anti-CSRF (synchronizer) token** is an unpredictable, per-session secret the server embeds in each form/page and requires back on every state-changing request. It defeats CSRF because the attacker's cross-site page **can't read the token** (the same-origin policy blocks it) and therefore can't include it. Spring Security generates and validates this automatically; the browser auto-sends the cookie, but only the legitimate page knows the matching token, so forged requests fail with **403**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the token works precisely because same-origin policy prevents the attacker reading it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the token is in a cookie alone (then it'd be auto-sent); not knowing it must come via a header/body the attacker can't set cross-site
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the synchronizer token pattern vs cookie-to-header (double-submit), and that Spring Security wires this in by default

sections.title: Why a Secret Token Defeats CSRF
sections.content:
A **CSRF token** (the **synchronizer token pattern**) is a random, unpredictable value tied to the user's session. The server **embeds it in every form/page** and **requires it back** on each state-changing request, usually as a hidden field or a request header.

Here's the crux: a CSRF attack relies on the browser **auto-attaching the cookie**, but it **cannot read content from another origin** because of the **same-origin policy**. The attacker's malicious page can submit a request to your site, but it **can't read your page's HTML** to extract the token — so it can't supply a valid one. The server sees a request with a session cookie but a **missing or wrong token**, and rejects it with **403**.

The token must travel in a place the attacker can't set cross-site — a **form field or custom header**, not just a plain cookie (a token only in a cookie would be auto-sent too). **Spring Security** generates, stores, and validates this token automatically for cookie/session apps; for SPAs it exposes it via a cookie your JS reads and echoes back in a header (the **cookie-to-header / double-submit** variant).

sections.title: Token Validation Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[Server renders form
with hidden _csrf token] --> B[Legit page submits
cookie + matching token] B --> C{Token present
and valid?} C -->|Yes| D[Request processed] A --> E[Attacker page submits
cookie but no token] E --> F[Same-origin policy blocks
reading the real token] F --> G{Token present?} G -->|No / wrong| H[403 Forbidden
forgery blocked] ```

sections.title: Vulnerable: CSRF disabled, no token required
Safe: Spring Security CSRF token (default + SPA setup)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Token only in a cookie**: a plain cookie is auto-sent, so it adds no protection. It must come via a **field or header** the attacker can't set cross-site.
- **Reusing a global/static token**: it must be **unpredictable and per-session** so it can't be guessed.
- **Validating on GET**: only **state-changing** methods (POST/PUT/DELETE) need the token; GET should be side-effect-free.
- **Disabling CSRF on a cookie app to 'fix' 403s**: that removes protection — instead, send the token correctly.
- **Confusing it with auth**: the token proves the *request came from your page*, not who the user is.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- A CSRF token is an **unpredictable, per-session secret** required on every state-changing request.
- It works because the **same-origin policy stops the attacker reading the token** from your page.
- It must travel as a **form field or header** — not only a cookie, which would be auto-sent.
- **Spring Security generates and validates it by default**; SPAs use the cookie-to-header variant.
- A missing/invalid token yields **403 Forbidden**, blocking the forged request.
- The token authenticates the **request's origin**, not the user.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
An anti-CSRF token, sometimes called a synchronizer token, is an unpredictable secret value that the server ties to the user's session. The server embeds it in every form or page it renders, and then it requires that same token back on every state-changing request — usually as a hidden form field or a custom header. If the token is missing or doesn't match, the request is rejected with a 403.

The reason this works is the heart of the answer. A CSRF attack depends on the browser automatically attaching the session cookie. But a malicious page on another domain cannot read the contents of your page, because of the browser's same-origin policy. So even though the attacker's page can fire a request at your site and the cookie gets attached automatically, the attacker has no way to read your real page to extract the token. Without the correct token, the server rejects the request. The legitimate page, on the other hand, was served by your server with the token baked in, so it can send it back.

One subtlety I'd mention is that the token has to travel somewhere the attacker can't set from another origin — a form field or a request header — not just a plain cookie. If the token were only in a cookie, it would get auto-sent just like the session cookie, and it wouldn't protect anything. For a single-page app, Spring Security supports a cookie-to-header pattern: it puts the token in a cookie that your own JavaScript reads and echoes back in a header, which a cross-site page can't do. The nice part is that Spring Security generates, stores, and validates all of this automatically for cookie-based apps — it's on by default.

beats.label: synchronizer token pattern
beats.content:
Here's how Spring Security's default approach works:
- User loads the form; Spring generates a random token and stores it in the session
- Token is embedded as a hidden field in the HTML form
- When the user submits, the token travels with the POST body
- Spring compares: token in request vs token in session
- They match — request allowed. They don't match — rejected
- Attacker on evil.com can't read your session token due to Same Origin Policy, so their forged form never has the right value

beats.label: spa variant
beats.content: For SPAs using AJAX, the double-submit cookie pattern works: the server sets the token in a readable cookie, the JavaScript reads it and adds it as a custom header (X-XSRF-TOKEN). Attackers can't forge custom headers on cross-origin requests.

beats.label: non-obvious
beats.content: non-obvious: the CSRF token doesn't need to be secret from the legitimate user. It just needs to be unguessable and unreadable cross-origin. The security comes from Same Origin Policy blocking evil.com from reading it.

question: Why are stateless REST APIs with JWT not vulnerable to CSRF?
title: CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: Stateless JWT APIs are largely immune to CSRF because the token is sent in the **`Authorization: Bearer` header**, which the browser does **not** attach automatically — so a malicious cross-site page **can't forge an authenticated request**. CSRF depends on **ambient credentials** (cookies auto-sent by the browser); when there are none, there's nothing to forge. The big caveat: if you store the JWT in a **cookie** instead of a header, the browser auto-sends it again and **CSRF is back** — so cookie-stored JWTs still need CSRF protection.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand CSRF immunity comes from NOT using auto-sent cookies, and that storing JWT in a cookie reintroduces the risk
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Stating 'JWT is immune to CSRF' unconditionally, ignoring the cookie-storage caveat; or disabling CSRF without understanding why
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Tie it together: header-based credentials require explicit JS to send, which same-origin policy prevents cross-site; cookie storage breaks that

sections.title: No Ambient Cookie, No CSRF
sections.content:
CSRF works by abusing **ambient authority** — credentials the browser **attaches automatically**, like a session cookie. A **stateless JWT API** typically sends the token in the **`Authorization: Bearer <jwt>` header**, which the browser **never adds on its own**; your JavaScript has to set it explicitly.

That explicit step is exactly what a cross-site attacker **can't perform**. A malicious page can fire a request at your API, but the **same-origin policy** prevents its JavaScript from reading your token or setting arbitrary headers on a cross-origin request. With no auto-sent credential and no way to add the header, **there's nothing to forge** — which is why it's standard and safe to **disable Spring Security's CSRF filter** for these APIs.

The essential caveat: this immunity comes from **where you store and send the token**, not from JWT itself. If you store the JWT in a **cookie**, the browser auto-sends it like any session cookie, and **CSRF is fully back** — so cookie-stored JWTs require CSRF protection (token or `SameSite`).

sections.title: CSRF Exposure by Token Storage
sections.content:
emerald|Authorization header|~CSRF-safe|JS sets it explicitly|browser never auto-adds|attacker can't forge
rose|JWT in cookie|~CSRF-exposed|browser auto-sends it|same as a session|needs CSRF token/SameSite
blue|Why it works|~Same-origin policy|blocks reading the token|blocks cross-origin headers|no ambient credential
amber|Practical rule|~Match defense to storage|header -> disable CSRF filter|cookie -> keep CSRF on|don't disable blindly

sections.title: Risky: JWT in an auto-sent cookie, CSRF disabled
Safe: stateless API, token in Authorization header
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **"JWT is immune to CSRF" with no caveat**: only true when the token is in a header, not a cookie.
- **JWT in a cookie + CSRF disabled**: the worst combination — re-enables CSRF and removes the defense.
- **Disabling CSRF on a session app**: that's a cookie-based app, so disabling CSRF opens it up.
- **Forgetting CORS**: CSRF immunity isn't CORS; you still configure CORS correctly for cross-origin SPAs.
- **Assuming localStorage is strictly better**: it dodges CSRF but is readable by XSS — a different trade-off.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- CSRF needs **ambient credentials**; a header-based JWT is **not auto-sent**, so there's nothing to forge.
- The **same-origin policy** stops an attacker's page reading your token or setting the header cross-site.
- It's therefore **safe and standard to disable CSRF** for stateless, header-token APIs.
- **Storing the JWT in a cookie reintroduces CSRF** — keep CSRF protection (`SameSite`/token) then.
- Immunity comes from **how the token is sent**, not from JWT itself.
- Don't confuse this with **CORS**, which is a separate cross-origin control.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Stateless JWT APIs are largely immune to CSRF, but it's important to explain why, because the immunity isn't automatic. CSRF works by abusing what's called ambient authority — credentials that the browser attaches to requests automatically, like a session cookie. With a typical stateless JWT API, you send the token in the Authorization header as a Bearer token, and the browser never adds that header on its own. Your JavaScript has to set it explicitly on each request.

That explicit step is exactly what a cross-site attacker can't do. A malicious page can certainly fire a request at your API, but the same-origin policy stops its JavaScript from reading your token or from setting a custom header on a cross-origin request. So there's no credential being sent automatically, and no way for the attacker to add one. With nothing to forge, the attack just doesn't apply — and that's why it's standard practice, and perfectly safe, to disable Spring Security's CSRF filter for this kind of API.

But here's the caveat I'd always add, because interviewers look for it: the immunity comes from how you store and send the token, not from JWT itself. If you decide to store the JWT in a cookie instead of sending it in a header, the browser will auto-attach that cookie to every request, just like a session cookie — and CSRF is fully back. So a cookie-stored JWT still needs CSRF protection, like an anti-CSRF token or SameSite cookies. The worst combination is putting the JWT in a cookie and also disabling CSRF, because then you've removed the protection while keeping the thing that's vulnerable.

beats.label: why cookies are the problem
beats.content: Browsers automatically attach cookies to every request to a domain, even from a different site. That automatic behavior is what CSRF exploits. An attacker on evil.com triggers a request to your API and the browser helpfully sends along your session cookie.

beats.label: why jwt in headers is safe
beats.content: Custom headers like Authorization: Bearer are not auto-attached. Browsers don't add them to cross-origin requests. An attacker's form can POST to your API, but that request arrives with no Authorization header. Your JWT filter sees no token and returns 401. The forged request dies there.

beats.label: production trap
beats.content: production trap: if you store the JWT in an HttpOnly cookie instead of the Authorization header, CSRF risk comes back. The browser auto-attaches the cookie again. In that case re-enable CSRF protection or add SameSite=Strict to the cookie.

question: What is the SameSite cookie attribute and how does it prevent CSRF?
title: CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: The **`SameSite` cookie attribute** tells the browser whether to send a cookie on **cross-site** requests. `SameSite=Strict` never sends it cross-site; `SameSite=Lax` (the modern default) sends it only on top-level GET navigations, not on cross-site POSTs or background requests; `SameSite=None` always sends it (and requires `Secure`). It mitigates CSRF by **stopping the session cookie from being auto-attached to forged cross-site requests**, cutting off CSRF's core mechanism — though it's a **defense in depth** layer, not a full replacement for anti-CSRF tokens.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the three SameSite values and that Lax/Strict block the auto-sent cookie that CSRF relies on
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing Lax is the modern browser default; treating SameSite as a complete CSRF fix; forgetting None requires Secure
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why Lax still allows top-level GET navigation (usability) and why you keep CSRF tokens as well for older browsers/edge cases

sections.title: Controlling When Cookies Cross Sites
sections.content:
The **`SameSite`** attribute on a cookie controls whether the browser includes it on **cross-site** requests — requests initiated by a different site than the cookie's owner. Since CSRF depends entirely on the browser **auto-attaching the session cookie** to a forged cross-site request, restricting that behavior strikes at CSRF's core.

There are three values: **`Strict`** never sends the cookie on any cross-site request (most secure, but breaks following inbound links while logged in); **`Lax`** — the **modern browser default** — sends it only on **top-level GET navigations** (clicking a link to your site) but **not** on cross-site POSTs, iframes, or background `fetch`/`img` requests, which is where CSRF lives; **`None`** always sends it and **must** be paired with **`Secure`** (HTTPS).

For most apps, **`Lax` already blocks the typical CSRF vector** (a cross-site POST) while keeping normal navigation working. Still, treat it as **defense in depth** alongside anti-CSRF tokens — older browsers and certain GET-based edge cases mean you don't rely on `SameSite` alone.

sections.title: SameSite Values at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Strict|~Most secure|never sent cross-site|blocks all CSRF vectors|breaks inbound logged-in links
blue|Lax (default)|~Balanced|sent on top-level GET nav|blocks cross-site POST|stops typical CSRF
rose|None|~Least restrictive|always sent cross-site|requires Secure + HTTPS|needed for cross-site embeds
amber|Role|~Defense in depth|complements CSRF tokens|not a full replacement|set on the session cookie

sections.title: Vulnerable: session cookie with no SameSite control
sections.content:
```properties
# Spring Boot: default before tuning — cookie may be sent cross-site
# (relying on browser default; older browsers historically sent cross-site)
server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site=none   # worst case: always cross-site
server.servlet.session.cookie.secure=false
```
*A cookie freely sent cross-site is exactly what a CSRF attack needs.*

sections.title: Safe: SameSite=Lax (or Strict) + Secure
sections.content:
```properties
# Block the session cookie on cross-site POSTs / background requests
server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site=lax    # or 'strict' for sensitive apps
server.servlet.session.cookie.secure=true       # HTTPS only
server.servlet.session.cookie.http-only=true    # also blocks JS access (XSS)
```
```java
// Or set it explicitly on a custom cookie
ResponseCookie cookie = ResponseCookie.from("SESSION", value)
    .httpOnly(true).secure(true).sameSite("Lax").path("/").build();
response.addHeader(HttpHeaders.SET_COOKIE, cookie.toString());
```
*With `Lax`, a cross-site POST to your transfer endpoint won't carry the session cookie — the forged request is unauthenticated.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating SameSite as a complete CSRF fix**: it's strong but a **defense in depth** layer — keep anti-CSRF tokens.
- **Not knowing `Lax` is the default**: modern browsers default to `Lax`, which already blocks cross-site POST CSRF.
- **`None` without `Secure`**: browsers reject `SameSite=None` cookies that aren't `Secure`.
- **Using `Strict` everywhere**: it logs users out when they follow inbound links — bad UX for content sites.
- **Confusing SameSite with HttpOnly**: `HttpOnly` blocks JS reading the cookie (XSS); `SameSite` controls cross-site sending (CSRF).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`SameSite`** controls whether a cookie is sent on **cross-site** requests.
- **`Strict`** = never cross-site; **`Lax`** (default) = only top-level GET nav; **`None`** = always (needs `Secure`).
- It mitigates CSRF by **stopping the session cookie auto-attaching to forged cross-site requests**.
- **`Lax` already blocks the typical CSRF POST vector** while keeping navigation usable.
- It's **defense in depth** — combine with **anti-CSRF tokens**, don't rely on it alone.
- In Spring Boot set it via `server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site` (plus `secure` + `http-only`).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The SameSite cookie attribute controls whether the browser will send a cookie on cross-site requests — that is, requests that were initiated by a different site than the one that owns the cookie. This matters for CSRF because CSRF depends entirely on the browser automatically attaching your session cookie to a forged cross-site request. If you stop that from happening, you've cut off the attack at its source.

There are three values. Strict means the cookie is never sent on any cross-site request — it's the most secure, but it has a usability cost, because even clicking a legitimate link to your site from somewhere else won't carry the session, so the user looks logged out. Lax, which is the modern browser default, is the balanced option: it sends the cookie on top-level GET navigations, like clicking a link, but it does not send it on cross-site POSTs, iframes, or background requests like images and fetch — and that's exactly where CSRF lives. So Lax already blocks the typical CSRF vector. The third value is None, which always sends the cookie cross-site, and browsers require it to be paired with the Secure flag so it only goes over HTTPS.

For most applications, setting the session cookie to Lax already stops the classic cross-site POST forgery while keeping normal navigation working. That said, I'd describe SameSite as defense in depth rather than a complete fix — older browsers and some GET-based edge cases mean I'd still keep anti-CSRF tokens enabled as well. In a Spring Boot app, you can set this with the server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site property, and I'd combine it with Secure and HttpOnly on the same cookie.

beats.label: lax is the sweet spot
beats.content: Lax is the modern browser default and it handles most CSRF scenarios. It blocks cross-site POSTs, AJAX, and embedded requests — the primary CSRF attack vectors. It still allows someone to click a link in an email and land on your site while logged in, which is expected behavior.

beats.label: non-obvious
beats.content: non-obvious: because browsers now default to Lax, many apps get baseline CSRF protection for free without any config change. But you should still set it explicitly in Spring Boot with server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site=Strict so behavior is guaranteed, not browser-dependent.

question: When should you disable CSRF protection in Spring Security?
title: CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: Disable CSRF protection **only when your app doesn't rely on auto-sent cookies for authentication** — i.e. a **stateless API** where each request carries credentials in the **`Authorization` header** (JWT, API key, OAuth bearer). With no ambient cookie to forge, CSRF doesn't apply, so the token filter is unnecessary overhead. **Keep CSRF enabled** for anything cookie/session-based (form login, server-rendered pages, or a JWT stored in a cookie). The deciding question is: *does the browser attach my credential automatically?*

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can state the precise condition for disabling CSRF (no cookie-based ambient auth) rather than 'disable it for REST APIs'
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Blanket 'disable CSRF for all REST APIs' even when the API uses session cookies; or disabling it to silence 403s on a session app
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame it as a single test — is authentication carried by an auto-sent cookie? — and note JWT-in-cookie is the trap

sections.title: The One Question That Decides It
sections.content:
Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default, and freshers often parrot "disable it for REST APIs." That's **only half right**. The real test is a single question: **does the browser send my authentication credential automatically?**

If authentication rides on an **auto-sent cookie** (form login, server-rendered pages, or even a **JWT stored in a cookie**), then CSRF applies and you **must keep protection on**. If each request instead carries credentials **explicitly** — a **JWT or API key in the `Authorization` header** — the browser attaches nothing on its own, a cross-site page can't forge the header, and **CSRF simply doesn't apply**. In that case the CSRF filter is pure overhead and you can safely disable it.

So: **disable CSRF for stateless, header-credential APIs; keep it for anything cookie-based.** The classic trap is a "REST API" that actually uses **session cookies** or a **JWT-in-cookie** — those are cookie-based and still need CSRF protection. Never disable CSRF just to silence a 403 on a session app.

sections.title: Enable or Disable? Decide by Credential Transport
sections.content:
rose|Cookie / session auth|~Keep CSRF ON|form login|server-rendered pages|JWT stored in a cookie
emerald|Header credential|~Safe to disable|JWT in Authorization|API key header|OAuth2 bearer token
amber|The deciding test|~One question|is the credential auto-sent?|cookie = yes, keep on|header = no, can disable
blue|Common trap|~Looks stateless, isn't|REST API on sessions|JWT-in-cookie|still needs CSRF

sections.title: Wrong: disabling CSRF on a cookie/session app
sections.content:
```java
// Form login uses the session cookie -> this app NEEDS CSRF protection
http.formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())
    .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable());   // BUG: opens the app to CSRF to silence 403s
```
*The session cookie is auto-sent, so disabling CSRF here makes every POST forgeable.*

sections.title: Right: disable only for stateless header-token APIs
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **"Disable CSRF for all REST APIs"**: wrong if the API authenticates with session cookies or JWT-in-cookie.
- **Disabling CSRF to fix a 403**: on a session app the 403 means your form is missing the token — send it instead.
- **JWT-in-cookie + CSRF disabled**: cookie is auto-sent, so this is forgeable. Keep CSRF on.
- **Assuming stateless = no cookies**: confirm credentials are in the **header**, not a cookie.
- **Disabling globally when only some endpoints are stateless**: scope it precisely if you mix styles.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Disable CSRF **only when authentication is not carried by an auto-sent cookie**.
- **Stateless APIs with header credentials** (JWT/API key/OAuth bearer) can safely disable it.
- **Keep CSRF on** for form login, server-rendered pages, and **JWT-stored-in-cookie**.
- The deciding test: **does the browser attach the credential automatically?**
- "Disable for all REST APIs" is an **incomplete, risky** rule.
- Never disable CSRF just to **silence a 403** on a cookie-based app.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A lot of people answer this with disable CSRF for REST APIs, but that's only half right, and interviewers are usually probing for the precise condition. The real test comes down to one question: does the browser send my authentication credential automatically? CSRF only works because browsers auto-attach things like session cookies to cross-site requests. So if my authentication relies on an auto-sent cookie, CSRF applies and I have to keep protection on. If, instead, every request carries its credential explicitly — like a JWT or an API key in the Authorization header — then the browser attaches nothing on its own, a cross-site page can't set that header, and CSRF simply doesn't apply. In that case the CSRF filter is just overhead and it's safe to disable it.

So the rule I'd state is: disable CSRF for stateless APIs that authenticate with a header token, and keep it on for anything cookie-based — form login, server-rendered pages, or a JWT that you've stored in a cookie. That last one is the classic trap. People build what they call a REST API but then keep server-side sessions, or they store the JWT in a cookie for convenience. Both of those are cookie-based, the browser auto-sends them, and they absolutely still need CSRF protection. The worst mistake I see is disabling CSRF just to make a 403 go away on a session-based app — that 403 usually means your form isn't sending the token, and the fix is to send the token, not to remove the defense. So I always come back to that single question about whether the credential is auto-sent.

seo.metaTitle: CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery | Java Backend Security
seo.metaDescription: When to disable Spring Security CSRF protection. JWT in Authorization header = safe to disable. Cookie-based sessions = must keep CSRF. Decision framework.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with OWASP-compliant security
speakable_v2.hook: The honest rule for disabling CSRF isn't "it's a REST API" — it's "nothing my app trusts gets attached to requests automatically."

beats.label: disable when
beats.content: Disable CSRF when your API authenticates via the Authorization header — JWT Bearer tokens or API keys. Browsers don't auto-attach headers cross-site, so the CSRF attack vector doesn't exist. Also safe to disable for mobile backends and machine-to-machine APIs where no browser is involved.

beats.label: keep when
beats.content: Keep CSRF enabled when cookies carry the auth credential. That includes traditional session-based web apps and any setup where the JWT itself is stored in a cookie. The browser auto-attaches cookies regardless of origin, so the attack is possible and protection is needed.

beats.label: gotcha
beats.content: gotcha: many tutorials say 'disable CSRF for REST APIs' without the nuance. The correct rule is: disable when authentication is header-based. If you switch from JWT in header to JWT in cookie tomorrow, you must re-enable CSRF. Always leave a code comment explaining the condition.
